c.tagline: Centuries of history around every rainy corner.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Phone-snatching (moped/e-bike) and pickpocketing in the West End, Oxford St and on the Tube; tourist areas otherwise safe

hood_desc: The entertainment and government core, home to West End theaters, restaurants, LGBTQ+ nightlife in Soho, and landmarks like Westminster and Big Ben, perfect for sightseers and night owls.
A hip East London district known for street art, vintage shops, cocktail bars, and a thriving creative and tech scene, ideal for trendsetters, artists, and nightlife seekers.
An elegant, affluent area of grand white townhouses, world-class museums like the V&A and Natural History Museum, and upscale shopping, suiting culture lovers and luxury travelers.
A bohemian, alternative neighborhood famous for its sprawling markets, live music venues, and countercultural vibe, appealing to young travelers, music fans, and market hunters.
A picturesque, upscale area of pastel houses, the famous Portobello Road antiques market, and the Notting Hill Carnival, drawing romantics, shoppers, and film-fan tourists.

water.note: Tap water is treated and safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.pay: Just tap a contactless bank card or phone at the gates — fares are capped daily and weekly automatically. If you prefer a card, an Oyster costs £7 (non-refundable, ~US$9.50) from station ticket machines. Buses are cashless; a single bus ride is £1.75 with unlimited changes within an hour.
transit.hours: The Tube runs about 5am to midnight; the Night Tube runs all night Fri–Sat on several lines, and 24-hour night buses cover the city.

landmarks: Big Ben (Elizabeth Tower)
The clock tower at the north end of the Houses of Parliament whose chimes and Gothic Revival face are instantly recognizable worldwide.
Tower Bridge
A Victorian bascule bridge with twin neo-Gothic towers over the Thames, one of the most photographed bridges in the world.
Buckingham Palace
The monarch's official London residence, famous for the Changing of the Guard ceremony and its grand neoclassical facade.
Tower of London
A historic castle and former royal prison on the Thames, home to the Crown Jewels and famous ravens.
London Eye
A giant riverside observation wheel offering sweeping views over Westminster and the Thames, especially striking lit up at night.
Westminster Abbey
The Gothic abbey church that has hosted every English coronation since 1066 and the tombs of monarchs, poets, and scientists.
St Paul's Cathedral
Christopher Wren's baroque masterpiece crowned by a soaring dome, a defining feature of the City of London skyline.
British Museum
One of the world's greatest museums, holding treasures like the Rosetta Stone and Parthenon Marbles beneath a famous glass-roofed Great Court.
Trafalgar Square
A grand public square anchored by Nelson's Column and bronze lion statues, a hub for gatherings and street photography.
Houses of Parliament (Palace of Westminster)
The riverside seat of the UK Parliament, a sprawling Gothic Revival landmark best photographed from across the Thames alongside Big Ben.

train.note: Eurostar leaves from London St Pancras International — arrive 45–90 minutes early for passport control and security, as French/Belgian border checks happen before boarding. There are no international night trains from London; the Caledonian Sleeper (to Scotland) and Night Riviera (to Cornwall) are domestic sleepers from Euston and Paddington.

bus.note: Most international coaches leave from Victoria Coach Station; journeys cross the Channel via the Eurotunnel shuttle or Dover ferry, so allow 8–10 hours to Paris and bring your passport.

intl.op: sails from Dover, ~1h40m by train from London — P&O Ferries
sails from Harwich, incl. overnight crossing — Stena Line

ferry.note: No international ferries sail from London itself — the nearest passenger ports are Dover and Harwich, both reachable by direct train. Stena's Harwich route sells combined Rail & Sail tickets from any London station, and its night sailing has cabins.

half.name: Windsor Castle
half.blurb: People visit the world's oldest occupied castle and official royal residence just west of London.

half.name: Oxford
half.blurb: The historic university city draws visitors for its ancient colleges and honey-colored stone buildings.

half.name: Bath
half.blurb: Famous for its Roman baths and elegant Georgian crescents built from golden stone.

half.name: Stonehenge
half.blurb: The prehistoric stone circle remains one of the world's most iconic and mysterious monuments.

half.name: Cambridge
half.blurb: People come for the famous university, riverside colleges, and gentle punting along the Cam.

half.name: Cotswolds
half.blurb: Rolling hills dotted with honey-stone villages make this classic English countryside a favorite.
